population_segments.source_text: 14. Children and Adolescents:

population_segments.name: Children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes
population_segments.source_text: The management of diabetes in children and adolescents cannot simply be derived from care routinely provided to adults with diabetes.

population_segments.name: Children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes
population_segments.source_text: Type 1 diabetes is the most common form of diabetes in children and adolescents

population_segments.source_text: Less stringent A1C goals (such as <7% [<53 mmol/mol] or <7.5% [<58 mmol/mol]) may be appropriate for children and adolescents with diabetes who cannot articulate symptoms of hypoglycemia

population_segments.name: Young children (aged <6 years) with diabetes
population_segments.source_text: special consideration should be given to the risk of hypoglycemia in young children (aged <6 years) who are often unable to recognize, articulate, and/or manage hypoglycemia.
defining_characteristics: Unable to recognize, articulate, and/or manage hypoglycemia

population_segments.name: Children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes
population_segments.source_text: TYPE 2 DIABETES IN CHILDREN AND ADOLESCENTS

population_segments.name: Adolescents with type 2 diabetes who have class 2 obesity or higher
population_segments.source_text: Consider metabolic surgery for the treatment of adolescents with type 2 diabetes who have class 2 obesity or higher (BMI 35 to <40 kg/m² or 120% to <140% percentile for age and sex, whichever is lower) and who have elevated A1C and/or serious co-morbidities despite lifestyle and pharmacologic intervention.
defining_characteristics: Class 2 obesity or higher (BMI 35 to <40 kg/m² or 120% to <140% percentile for age and sex, whichever is lower)
Elevated A1C and/or serious co-morbidities despite lifestyle and pharmacologic intervention

population_segments.name: Adolescents with type 2 diabetes and BMI 40 kg/m² or higher
population_segments.source_text: Metabolic surgery for adolescents with type 2 diabetes should be considered for those with BMI 40 kg/m² or higher with or without comorbidities.

population_segments.name: Individuals with type 1 diabetes
population_segments.source_text: At diagnosis, ∼25% of children with type 1 diabetes have thyroid autoantibodies

population_segments.name: Individuals with type 1 diabetes and thyroid autoantibodies
population_segments.source_text: At diagnosis, ∼25% of children with type 1 diabetes have thyroid autoantibodies (172), the presence of which is predictive of thyroid dysfunction—most commonly hypothyroidism, although hyperthyroidism occurs in ∼0.5% of people with type 1 diabetes (173,174).

population_segments.name: Individuals with type 1 diabetes and celiac disease
population_segments.source_text: Celiac disease is an immune-mediated disorder that occurs with increased frequency in people with type 1 diabetes (1.6–16.4% of individuals compared with 0.3–1% in the general population) (165,168,169, 178–181).

population_segments.name: Children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes and dyslipidemia
population_segments.source_text: Youth with type 1 diabetes have a high prevalence of lipid abnormalities (192,199).

population_segments.name: Children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes
population_segments.source_text: Retinopathy (like albuminuria) most commonly occurs after the onset of puberty and after 5–10 years of diabetes duration (214).

population_segments.name: Children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes
population_segments.source_text: Diabetic neuropathy rarely occurs in prepubertal children or after only 1–2 years of diabetes (214), although data suggest a prevalence of distal peripheral neuropathy of 7% among 1,734 adolescents with type 1 diabetes in the SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth study and association with the presence of CVD risk factors (220,221).

population_segments.name: Children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes
population_segments.source_text: Data from 7,549 individuals <20 years of age in the T1D Exchange clinic registry emphasize the importance of meeting glycemic and blood pressure goals, particularly as diabetes duration increases, to reduce the risk of chronic kidney disease.

population_segments.name: Children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes
population_segments.source_text: Type 2 diabetes in children and adolescents is associated with significant microvascular and macrovascular risk burden and a substantial increase in the risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality at an earlier age than in those diagnosed later in life (13,223).

specific_goals.name: A1C goal for most children and adolescents with diabetes
specific_goals.rationale: appropriate for most children and adolescents with diabetes. B

specific_goals.name: Less stringent A1C goal for children and adolescents with diabetes
specific_goals.rationale: may be appropriate for children and adolescents with diabetes who cannot articulate symptoms of hypoglycemia; have hypoglycemia unawareness; cannot access advanced insulin delivery technology and/or CGM; cannot check blood glucose regularly; or have nonglycemic factors that increase A1C. B

specific_goals.name: A1C goal for children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes
specific_goals.rationale: For children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes, glycemic status should be assessed at least every 3 months or as frequently as clinically indicated. Consider setting an A1C goal of <6.5% (<48 mmol/mol) for most children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes who have a low risk of hypoglycemia. For those at higher risk of hypoglycemia, A1C goals should be individualized as clinically appropriate.

specific_goals.name: Blood glucose goal prior to physical activity and exercise
specific_goals.rationale: but should be individualized based on the insulin plan and type, intensity, and duration of activity (36,115).

allowed_medications.name: Metformin for children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes
allowed_medications.special_instructions: Initiate pharmacologic therapy with consideration of multiple add-on therapies early on, in addition to behavioral counseling for healthful nutrition and physical activity changes, at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. In individuals with incidentally diagnosed type 2 diabetes (A1C <8.5% [ <69 mmol/mol] and asymptomatic), metformin is the initial pharmacologic treatment of choice unless contraindicated by kidney function.

allowed_medications.name: Insulin for children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes
allowed_medications.special_instructions: Children and adolescents with marked hyperglycemia (A1C ≥8.5% [≥69 mmol/mol]) without acidosis at diagnosis should be treated initially with long-acting insulin while metformin is initiated and titrated. Initiate subcutaneous or intravenous insulin treatment in individuals with ketoacidosis to rapidly correct the hyperglycemia and the metabolic derangement. Once acidosis is resolved, metformin should be initiated while subcutaneous insulin therapy is continued.

allowed_medications.name: GLP-1 receptor agonist for children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes
allowed_medications.special_instructions: If individualized glycemic goals are not achieved or maintained with metformin (with or without long-acting insulin), glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) and/or sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2is) should be considered.

allowed_medications.name: SGLT2 inhibitor for children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes
allowed_medications.special_instructions: If individualized glycemic goals are not achieved or maintained with metformin (with or without long-acting insulin), glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) and/or sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2is) should be considered.
